title: How Motivation Relates to Generative AI Use: A Large-Scale Survey of Mexican High School Students
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how high school students’ motivational profiles relate to their use of generative AI tools in two academic domains: math and writing. The core question is not whether ChatGPT or another AI intervention improves learning outcomes, but how students with different levels of self-concept and perceived subject value differ in the ways they report using generative AI. The study is framed by situated expectancy-value theory and aims to inform more tailored AI integration strategies in education.

The study used an anonymous online survey administered to students in the final two years of public high school in Chihuahua, Mexico. After excluding students who failed attention checks or had no prior generative AI experience, the analytic sample was 6,793 students. Students self-reported their motivation in math and writing and their frequency of using AI for specific tasks such as brainstorming, outlining, grammar improvement, writing feedback, problem interpretation, and answer copying. The researchers then applied K-means clustering separately in math and writing to identify motivational profiles and compared AI-use patterns across those clusters.

Three profiles emerged in both subject areas: Aspirational, Confident, and Disengaged. In writing, Aspirational students most often used AI for brainstorming and outlining, Confident students most often used it for grammar improvement and writing feedback, and Disengaged students reported the lowest overall use across most writing tasks. In math, Aspirational students used AI more as a compensatory tutor, Confident students used it more selectively and for refinement, and Disengaged students showed relatively more shortcut-seeking behavior such as direct answer copying.

The paper concludes that AI use among students is domain-specific and varies meaningfully by motivational profile, challenging one-size-fits-all assumptions about AI integration in schools. Importantly for evidence synthesis, this is not a randomized or quasi-experimental intervention study, does not include treatment and control groups, and does not report learning or motivation gains over time. It therefore does not match the alleged 2026 25-plus-25 student 12-week high-school writing ChatGPT trial, provides no original pre/post statistics on motivation or writing performance, and should be excluded from any quantitative synthesis of ChatGPT-based writing feedback effects in high school.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a large cross-sectional survey with clustering and pairwise comparisons, not a randomized trial or quasi-experiment. It provides useful descriptive evidence on associations between motivation profiles and AI use, but it does not support causal claims about ChatGPT improving motivation or writing.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no intervention effect sizes on motivation or writing achievement, so impact is unclear rather than demonstrated. Any practical implications are inferential and descriptive, not based on measured pre-post learning gains or experimental treatment effects.

interventions.use_case: Surveying Mexican high school students' self-reported use of generative AI/ChatGPT-like tools for math help and writing support, including brainstorming, outlining, grammar improvement, and writing feedback.
Writing-domain uses of generative AI as a writing assistant for brainstorming, outline generation, language/grammar improvement, adapting text to requirements, and obtaining writing feedback.

finding.finding_summary: This was a cross-sectional survey of 6,793 Mexican high school students, not an intervention study. K-means clustering identified three motivational profiles (Aspirational, Confident, Disengaged) based on self-concept and perceived subject value in math and writing, and these profiles were associated with different self-reported AI usage patterns; no causal effect of AI on motivation was estimated and no standardized effect size for motivation outcomes was reported.
finding.measure: Self-concept and perceived subject value survey items (5-item self-concept, 3-item subject value; 1-7 scales), used to derive motivational profiles via K-means clustering

finding.finding_summary: In the writing domain, students in different motivational clusters reported different frequencies of generative AI use for literacy-related tasks rather than different writing achievement outcomes. Aspirational students most frequently reported AI use for brainstorming ideas (M=2.83) and producing outlines (M=2.72), while Confident students reported the highest use for language/grammar improvement (M=2.79) and writing feedback (M=2.67); no writing performance test, gain score, or experimental effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Self-reported frequency of AI use for writing tasks on 1-5 Likert scales (brainstorming, outline production, supporting evidence, language/grammar improvement, writing feedback, requirement adaptation)
finding.study_size: n=6793; writing clusters: Aspirational n=3191, Confident n=1915, Disengaged n=1687

finding.finding_summary: In math, motivational profiles were associated with distinct self-reported AI usage patterns, but no math learning outcome was experimentally tested. Aspirational students reported the highest use of AI for step-by-step guides (M=2.81) and problem interpretation (M=2.59), while Disengaged students reported the highest direct answer copying (M=2.69), significantly above Aspirational (M=2.53, p<.001) and Confident students (M=2.18, p<.001).
finding.measure: Self-reported frequency of AI use for math tasks on 1-5 Likert scales (formula retrieval, direct answer copying, problem interpretation, step-by-step guides, solution verification, practice generation)
finding.study_size: n=6793; math clusters: Aspirational n=2809, Confident n=2207, Disengaged n=1777
